1.title: AI Policies, Governance and Ethics
1.text: Welcome to Module fourteen: A I Policies, Governance and Ethics. This module covers a i policies, governance and ethics. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. What an organizational A I policy contains and how to follow it. Governance roles and controls: owners, approvals, logging, review. The ethical issues in everyday A I use: honesty, fairness, privacy, accountability, transparency. How to act when a request conflicts with policy or ethics.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's AI Use Policy
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's A I Use Policy. After a pilot, Cedarbrook publishes a one-page A I use policy: approved tools and accounts, data rules, what must be reviewed, how to disclose A I use, who to ask. A new analyst wants to use a free tool they found online; the policy says to use only the approved Claude workspace.

1.title: Organizational AI Policies
1.text: Organizational A I Policies. An A I policy turns principles into rules for daily work. Typical parts.

1.title: Organizational AI Policies, continued
1.text: Organizational A I Policies, continued. The figure shows this: A typical A I policy covers approved tools and accounts, data rules, allowed and prohibited uses, review, disclosure, and who to contact.

1.title: Organizational AI Policies, continued
1.text: Organizational A I Policies, continued. Approved tools and accounts. What it says: Which A I tools, plans and workspaces may be used. Your duty: Use only those; no personal accounts for company data. Data rules. What it says: What data may enter A I tools (Module thirteen). Your duty: Classify, minimize, anonymize. Allowed and prohibited uses. What it says: Examples of each. Your duty: Check before starting a new kind of use. Review requirements. What it says: When a person must check outputs, and who. Your duty: Follow the review steps; keep a record. Disclosure. What it says: When to tell customers, colleagues or regulators that A I was used. Your duty: Disclose as required.

1.title: Organizational AI Policies, continued
1.text: Organizational A I Policies, continued. Intellectual property. What it says: Ownership and use of A I outputs and of third-party material. Your duty: Do not paste others' confidential or copyrighted material improperly. Training and access. What it says: Who may use which features (connectors, Skills, file creation). Your duty: Complete training; respect feature limits. Incident reporting. What it says: What to do when something goes wrong (data leak, harmful output). Your duty: Report quickly to the named contact. Policy first. Product features and settings do not override your organization's rules. If the policy and a tool's capability differ, follow the policy.

1.title: Organizational AI Policies, continued
1.text: Organizational A I Policies, continued. Admins control what is available: on Team and Enterprise plans owners can enable or restrict web search, connectors, Skills, file creation, sharing and memory. When the policy does not cover your case, ask the policy owner before proceeding. Exam tip: In policy scenarios, the correct choice usually follows the written policy and approved tools, asks the policy owner when it is silent, and reports incidents promptly.

1.title: Governance in Practice
1.text: Governance in Practice. Governance is the set of roles, rules and checks that keep A I use safe, lawful and valuable.

1.title: Governance in Practice, continued
1.text: Governance in Practice, continued. Ownership. Each Project, Skill and shared prompt has a named owner. Approval. New use cases and connectors are approved before rollout. Risk tiers. Low (internal drafts), medium (customer-facing text), high (decisions about people, regulated content) with matching review. Human oversight. A qualified person reviews outputs in medium and high tiers. Records. Log of high-risk uses, reviewers and decisions. Quality checks. Sample reviews of outputs; tracked error rate. Training. Short course for all users, with examples. Change control. Instructions and knowledge updated by the owner, tested and logged (Module twelve).

1.title: Governance in Practice, continued
1.text: Governance in Practice, continued. Incident response. Defined steps for data leaks or harmful output. Review cycle. Policy revisited as tools and laws change.

1.title: Governance in Practice, continued
1.text: Governance in Practice, continued. The figure shows this: Governance turns principles into policy, and policy into controls and checks, with people accountable at every level. Accountability stays with people. An A I cannot be held responsible; the person who uses or approves the output is. Proportionate controls. More review for higher risk; avoid heavy process on low-risk tasks.

1.title: Ethics of Everyday AI Use
1.text: Ethics of Everyday A I Use. Honesty and transparency. Meaning: Do not mislead people about A I involvement or about what the output is. Examples: Disclose A I-assisted content when required; do not present invented sources as real; do not impersonate. Fairness. Meaning: Avoid unfair treatment and bias. Examples: Review hiring, grading and customer-service outputs for bias; do not let Claude make people decisions alone. Privacy. Meaning: Respect the people behind the data. Examples: Minimize, anonymize, follow consent. Accountability. Meaning: A named person owns the result. Examples: Review before sending; keep records. Safety and non-harm. Meaning: Avoid content or actions that could hurt people. Examples: Do not use Claude to deceive, harass or defraud.

1.title: Ethics of Everyday AI Use, continued
1.text: Ethics of Everyday A I Use, continued. Respect for creators. Meaning: Do not misuse others' work. Examples: Check copyright and licensing; cite sources. Human dignity and judgment. Meaning: Keep people in control of decisions about people. Examples: Human review for high-stakes cases. Reliability. Meaning: Do not overstate what A I can do. Examples: Communicate limits; verify. Common dilemmas. Passing off A I work as purely your own where disclosure is expected (school, publication, client work with a disclosure clause). Using A I-generated reviews, testimonials or fake personas to influence customers (deceptive, prohibited). Automating a decision about a person (hiring, credit, discipline) without human review.

1.title: Ethics of Everyday AI Use, continued
1.text: Ethics of Everyday A I Use, continued. Feeding an employee's or customer's private information into a tool without a legitimate basis. Generating realistic content that could mislead (fake quotes, edited images presented as real). Over-trusting outputs in safety, medical or legal contexts. Anthropic's Usage Policy requires disclosure to affected people in high-risk uses and expects consumer-facing chatbots to say they are A I. Claude's output may carry marks (invisible text watermarks and content credentials for files) so provenance can sometimes be checked; absence of a mark proves nothing.

2.title: Ethics of Everyday AI Use, continued
2.text: Ethics of Everyday A I Use, continued. The Associate does not need to resolve every ethical question alone: spot the issue, apply the policy and escalate (to a manager, Legal, Privacy or an ethics contact). Exam tip: Ethical-scenario answers favor transparency, fairness checks, human accountability and privacy. Options that hide A I use, skip review of people decisions or fabricate content are wrong.

2.title: When Your Request Conflicts with Policy
2.text: When Your Request Conflicts with Policy. Stop before sharing data or sending output. Check the policy and the data class. Choose a compliant path: remove sensitive data, use the approved tool, add human review, or change the task. Ask the policy owner, Legal or Privacy if still unsure. Report any breach or near miss at once. Record the decision. Exam tip: Policy first, then people: follow the approved tools and rules, ask the owner when the policy is silent, and report incidents quickly.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Policy first: Features do not override the organization's rules. Policy parts: Approved tools, data, allowed uses, review, disclosure, I P, training, incidents. When silent: Ask the policy owner, Legal or Privacy. Governance: Owners, approvals, risk tiers, human oversight, records, training, incident response. Accountability: People, not the A I. Ethics: Honesty, fairness, privacy, accountability, safety, respect for creators, human judgment, reliability. Red flags: Fake reviews or personas, automated people decisions, hiding A I use, private data without basis. High-risk uses: Qualified human review plus disclosure. Incident: Contain, report, record.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A new analyst wants to use a free A I website they found instead of the company's approved Claude workspace. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Approved tools and accounts are a core policy requirement.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. An employee notices that a chat shared earlier included a customer's phone number. What is the best next step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The right response is to contain the exposure by unsharing the chat and then report the incident promptly to the named contact.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A marketer wants Claude to create customer testimonials with invented names to post on the website. What is the correct response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Fake reviews and personas are prohibited deceptive activity.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Which statement about accountability is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. An A I system cannot be held responsible, so accountability stays with the people who use, review and approve its output.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. The A I policy does not mention using Claude to summarize supplier contracts. What should the employee do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. When policy is silent on a sensitive use, ask first.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Select two. Which two are ethical practices when using Claude to help screen job applications? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. Reviewing outputs for bias, keeping a qualified person as the decision-maker and being open about A I use are the fair and transparent practices.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A manager wants to present A I-drafted analysis as verified fact without checking it. What principle is breached? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Presenting unchecked output as verified fact overstates reliability, misleads readers and skips the verification that responsible use requires.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Which control best fits a high-risk use such as decisions about benefits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. High-risk uses require human oversight, accountability and transparency.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. An employee finds that Claude produced text closely matching a copyrighted article. What is the best action? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Respect creators' rights; verify originality and follow policy.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: D. Question two: A. Question three: C. Question four: A. Question five: C. Question six: A and E. Question seven: D. Question eight: D. Question nine: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
